sections.title: What actually drove instructor performance in September
subheadings: The five findings that should change decisions
sections.layout:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What actually drove instructor performance in September

Fourteen instructors taught 328 classes at Kwality House in September 2026, generating 2,090 check-ins at 45.4% capacity utilisation. On the surface Rohan Dahima "won" the month with 302 attendances — 14.4% of everything the studio delivered. This report tests whether that ranking survives scrutiny. It largely does not.

The single most important finding

After controlling for day of week, time of day, class format, room capacity and week of the month, only three of the fourteen instructors are statistically distinguishable from the roster average — and all three are distinguishable for being weak, not strong. Bret Saldanha (-1.56 attendees per class), Karanvir Bhatia (-1.29) and Raunak Khemuka (-3.49) carry genuine negative effects (p<0.05). The other eleven sit inside the noise band. The practical implication is that Kwality House's September result was determined far more by which slots existed and how they were formatted than by who stood at the front of the room — with one costly exception: the studio is carrying 70 classes a month on instructors who measurably under-deliver in them.

The five findings that should change decisions

1 · The instructor leaderboard is mostly a scheduling artefact — but the bottom of it is real
Observation
Raw average attendance per instructor ranges from 2.84 (Raunak Khemuka) to 8.44 (Reshma Sharma) — a 3× spread.
Evidence
A fixed-effects model on all 328 September classes (controlling for day, time band, format, log capacity and ISO week) explains 31.8% of attendance variance. Ten of the thirteen instructor coefficients are statistically indistinguishable from the roster average. Only three are significant and all three are negative: Raunak Khemuka −3.49, Bret Saldanha −1.56, Karanvir Bhatia −1.29.
Interpretation
Most of the apparent gap between instructors is the slot they were given, not the draw they exert. But three instructors lose roughly 1.3–3.5 attendees per class relative to what an average colleague would deliver in the identical slot.
Why it matters
Bret, Karanvir and Raunak together taught 75 of 328 classes (22.9%) and produced only 313 check-ins (15.0%). The measured deficit on those classes is roughly 147 attendances in one month.
Recommended action
Stop treating these three as interchangeable cover. Re-allocate their weakest recurring slots first (Monday 18:00 powerCycle, Monday 19:30 powerCycle, Saturday 16:30 powerCycle, Sunday 16:00 Barre 57) and redeploy to instructors with positive adjusted effects.
Expected outcome
Closing even half the measured gap on the 31 chronically sub-4.0 powerCycle classes would add ~75–95 monthly attendances.
Success metric
Roster-weighted average attendance per class ≥ 7.00 within two months, with no fall in total class count.
2 · Clients are slot-loyal, not instructor-loyal — which makes roster flexibility cheap
Observation
Instructor preference exists but is modest.
Evidence
Across the 474 clients who visited in September and attended two or more classes, the average share of a client's visits taken with their single most-attended instructor was 42.4%. A null model that randomly reassigns instructors while preserving each client's visit count and each instructor's overall popularity produces 35.7% — a lift of 1.19×.
Interpretation
Instructor affinity is real but accounts for only about one fifth of the concentration that a pure slot-driven schedule would not already produce. Clients book the 7:30 class; whoever teaches it is secondary.
Why it matters
This is the most commercially useful finding in the report: it means management can move instructors between slots — including removing weak ones — with far less demand risk than a "clients will follow the teacher" assumption would suggest.
Recommended action
Treat instructor changes as a low-risk lever. Validate with a controlled substitution protocol (see Report 04) rather than assuming lock-in.
Expected outcome
Greater freedom to optimise the roster on slot and format economics rather than on instructor politics.
Success metric
Client overlap in substituted slots stays within ±5pp of the 28.5% September baseline for unchanged slots.
3 · Rohan Dahima is the studio's load-bearing instructor — and that is a concentration risk, not a triumph
Observation
Rohan Dahima taught 40 classes (12.2% of the schedule) and drew 302 check-ins (14.4%).
Evidence
He is the only instructor who appears in the top three for every format he teaches: powerCycle 7.65 avg (vs 4.82 format average), Barre 8.19, Strength Lab 5.5. He also carries the highest load-adjusted resilience — his 40 classes span 14 distinct recurring slots and 17 separate days.
Interpretation
His headline number is partly volume (most classes) but his per-class performance is genuinely top-quartile in every format. He is doing the work of roughly 1.4 average instructors.
Why it matters
Instructor concentration is moderate in aggregate (Herfindahl 0.0851, effective N 11.75, top-3 share 34.7%), but the top three by attendance — Rohan, Pranjali Jain, Reshma Sharma — account for 34.7% of all check-ins. Losing any one of them to leave, illness or a competing studio would remove 8–14% of monthly attendance with no obvious internal replacement at that per-class level.
Recommended action
Build named understudies for Rohan's three highest-yield recurring slots (Wednesday 08:00 powerCycle, Tuesday 19:15 powerCycle, Thursday 18:00 powerCycle) and test them while he is still in place.
Expected outcome
Reduced single-point-of-failure risk; a measurable second-line bench.
Success metric
At least two other instructors each complete ≥4 classes in a Rohan-held slot at ≥85% of his trailing average, before any unplanned absence occurs.
4 · The instructors who "look" weakest on average are sometimes the best at hard slots
Observation
Anmol Sharma and Richard D'Costa have low total attendance but the highest average utilisation on the roster.
Evidence
Anmol Sharma: 14 classes, 61.6% utilisation — the highest of any instructor — because he is consistently assigned to small-capacity Strength Lab (capacity 7–10) rooms. His adjusted effect is 0.02, statistically indistinguishable from average.
Interpretation
Utilisation and total attendance answer different questions. Anmol fills small rooms; Cauveri Vikrant fills none (41.0%) because she is given 18–22 capacity barre rooms in soft slots.
Why it matters
Ranking on a single metric would have management demote Anmol and promote Cauveri. Both conclusions would be wrong.
Recommended action
Evaluate every instructor on schedule-adjusted effect, then on utilisation versus the capacity they were actually given, and only then on totals.
Expected outcome
Deployment decisions stop rewarding instructors who were simply handed better rooms.
Success metric
All instructor reviews cite the adjusted effect and the capacity-adjusted utilisation, not raw totals.
5 · New-client acquisition is the studio's weakest link and it sits with specific instructors
Observation
122 people took their first-ever Physique 57 class at Kwality House in September. Very few came back.
Evidence
Of those 122 first-timers, only 9.0% visited again within 21 days — the worst monthly conversion in the twelve months measured (June 2026 peaked at 25.7%). Cauveri Vikrant taught 36 of the 122 first-timers (29.5%) — but 30 of those arrived via hosted/corporate classes, so her apparent acquisition strength is an event artefact, not a conversion skill.
Interpretation
The studio is buying first visits through corporate hosted events and introductory offers, then failing to convert them. Hosted classes contributed 60 check-ins (2.9% of the month) at zero recorded revenue.
Why it matters
At a 9% 21-day conversion rate, acquisition spend is largely being wasted. Every percentage point of conversion is worth roughly 1.2 returning clients a month, compounding into the base.
Recommended action
Separate hosted-event attendance from organic trial in all reporting. Attach a named second-visit booking prompt to every first-timer, and measure conversion by the instructor who taught the first class.
Expected outcome
New-client 21-day return rate recovering from 9.0% toward the 18–20% achieved in March, May and June 2026.
Success metric
New-client 21-day return ≥15% for two consecutive months; hosted-class attendance reported separately from organic trial.

SECTION B

Schedule-adjusted performance: appeal or advantage?

A raw average conflates two things: how much demand an instructor personally attracts, and how much demand the slot they were handed already contains. To separate them we estimated an ordinary least squares model on all 328 September classes at Kwality House:

Attendance ~ instructor + day of week + time band + format + log(capacity) + ISO week

Day of week, time band and format enter as sum-to-zero contrasts; week controls for the studio-wide demand shift described in Report 02. Model R² = 0.318 on 328 observations. Instructor effects are then centred on the session-weighted roster average so they read as "attendees per class versus an average colleague in the same circumstances". Positive means the instructor out-draws the slot; negative means the slot was carrying them.

Reading this correctly

SECTION C

Instructor–client affinity and loyalty

Do clients follow teachers, or do they follow the clock? This matters directly: if clients are teacher-loyal, roster changes are dangerous; if they are slot-loyal, roster changes are one of the cheapest levers available.

Top-instructor concentration

Observed
42.4%
Random null
35.7%

Clients with ≥2 September visits (260 clients, 1,876 visits). Null model reshuffles instructors within each client's own visit history, preserving visit counts and instructor popularity.

Do clients ever see only one teacher?

Number of September clients at each visit frequency. Of the 55 clients who came exactly twice, only 12 stayed with a single instructor. Not one client who attended four or more classes used only one instructor.

Core-client share by instructor

Share of each instructor's September clients who visited Kwality House again in the 1–24 October window. Studio baseline 74.7% (excluding hosted classes, 76.9%).

Instructor changes are a lower-risk lever than management probably assumes
Observation
Clients who attend a recurring class do not stay with a single teacher once they visit more than twice.
Evidence
Zero of the 180 clients who attended four or more September classes used only one instructor. Of 55 two-visit clients, 12 (21.8%) were single-instructor. Observed top-instructor concentration of 42.4% is only 1.19× the 35.7% that a slot-driven schedule would generate by chance.
Interpretation
There is a real but modest instructor preference. It is not strong enough to make instructor redeployment commercially dangerous.
Why it matters
Management can optimise the roster on slot economics — moving people to where the demand is — instead of protecting incumbent assignments.
Recommended action
Run substitutions as controlled tests (Report 04 protocol) rather than avoiding them. Keep the slot and format constant and change only the instructor.
Expected outcome
A usable evidence base on instructor–slot fit within eight weeks.
Success metric
Client overlap in changed slots within ±5pp of the 28.5% September baseline measured on unchanged slots.

Deceptively strong headline: Rohan Dahima
302 check-ins is 14.4% of the studio's month, but 40 classes is 12.2% of the schedule, his adjusted effect (+0.63) is not statistically significant, and his client return rate (76.5%) is only mid-pack. His number is volume plus good slots, not a measurable personal premium. Protect him as capacity, not as a magic draw.
Deceptively weak headline: Anmol Sharma
14 classes and only 85 check-ins looks poor until you see 61.6% utilisation — the highest on the roster — because he is assigned to 7–10 capacity Strength Lab rooms. His adjusted effect (+0.02) is indistinguishable from average.
Declining despite a stable schedule: Karanvir Bhatia
Monthly average attendance: 5.09 (Jul 2026), 6.76 (Aug), 5.50 (Sep) on a rising class count (23 → 21 → 24). His adjusted effect of −1.29 is significant at p=0.018 and his client return rate is 63.6%, the second lowest. The schedule is not the problem.
Instructor fatigue signal: Bret Saldanha
32 classes in September (up from 30 in August) at 3.97 average — the second worst on the roster — and an adjusted effect of -1.56 (p=0.004). He is spread across 13 distinct recurring slots and 6 days a week with no single slot repeated more than 5 times. High dispersion plus high load plus weak outcomes is the classic signature of an instructor used as cover rather than as an anchor.
Concentration risk
Herfindahl index on attendance share is 0.0851 (effective N 11.75), and the top three instructors deliver 34.7% of all check-ins. Aggregate concentration is moderate, but it is concentrated in the instructors who also hold the strongest slots — so a single departure would remove both the teacher and the slot's demand.
Cover-instructor system
Cauveri Vikrant (18 distinct recurring slots in 23 classes), Richard D'Costa (8 slots in 8 classes) and Vivaran Dhasmana (11 in 18) function as floaters rather than anchors. This keeps the timetable covered but makes it impossible to build slot-level client habits, and it means no performance signal can ever accumulate for them in any single slot.

CRITICAL

What the headline numbers are not telling us

Six contradictions in the September instructor data

The instructor with the most attendance is not the best instructor
Rohan Dahima's 302 check-ins come from 40 classes — 12.2% of the schedule. Per class he delivers 7.55 against a studio average of 6.37, but his adjusted effect (+0.63, p not significant) says an average colleague in his slots would have delivered nearly as much. Reshma Sharma (25 classes, 8.44 avg, +0.35) and Vivaran Dhasmana (18 classes, 6.72 avg, +0.46) are doing more with less.
The highest utilisation on the roster belongs to one of its lowest-volume instructors
Anmol Sharma fills 61.6% of his capacity from just 85 check-ins, because his rooms seat 7–10. Cauveri Vikrant fills 41.0% from 141 check-ins because hers seat 18–22. Any ranking that mixes the two is measuring room size, not teaching.
The instructor with the most new clients converts almost none of them
Cauveri Vikrant taught 36 of the studio's 122 first-timers (29.5%) — the highest on the roster — but 30 of those arrived through hosted corporate classes. Her client return rate is 56.7%, the lowest on the roster, rising to 70.2% once hosted classes are stripped out. Reporting her as an acquisition leader would be wrong.
A strong average is hiding the studio's most volatile performer
Cauveri Vikrant's standard deviation across her 23 classes is 3.62 (CV 0.59) with a range of 1 to 18 — that 18 is a hosted corporate class. Richard D'Costa's CV is 0.81 across 8 classes. Volatility at this level means a single class tells you nothing, and neither does a single month.
Nobody is actually instructor-loyal above four visits
Zero of 180 clients with four or more September visits used a single instructor. The studio's repeat business is built on timetable habits and format preferences, not on teacher followings. Any strategy premised on teacher followings is premised on something the data does not show.
The bottom three are carrying a fifth of the schedule
Bret Saldanha, Karanvir Bhatia and Raunak Khemuka taught 75 classes (22.9%) for 313 check-ins (15.0%). Their combined measured deficit against a roster-average instructor in the same slots is roughly 147 attendances for the month — about 4.6% of total studio attendance, lost without a single cancelled class.

GOVERNANCE

Measurement framework

Five metrics govern the instructor actions recommended in this report. Each has a September baseline and a stated review point. The first two are new reporting requirements — without them the rest cannot be governed.

MetricSeptember 2026 baselineTargetCadenceWhy this metric
Schedule-adjusted instructor effectRange −3.49 to +1.21; 3 of 14 significantBottom tier improves to better than −0.80Quarterly, on a rolling quarter of dataThe only instructor measure that is not confounded by which slots an instructor was given. Recomputed quarterly, not monthly — monthly samples are too small.
Share of classes taught by the bottom tier75 of 328 (22.9%)Below 15%MonthlyThe single clearest measure of whether the reallocation has actually happened, rather than been discussed.
Client return rate by instructorStudio 74.7%; range 56.7% to 85.9%No instructor below 65% excl. hostedMonthlySeparates retention skill from attendance volume. Must be reported excluding hosted classes, which distort it.
New-client 21-day return rate9.0%≥15% for two consecutive monthsMonthly, cohort-basedLagging by design. Judge on cohorts, not on monthly snapshots.
Instructor concentration (Herfindahl)0.085 — effective N 11.75Effective N maintained at 10 or aboveMonthlyRising concentration means growing key-person risk even while attendance looks healthy.

How to measure an instructor change

  • Change only the instructor. Hold day, time and format constant, or the result is uninterpretable.
  • Compare against same-day unchanged slots. In September that control was −1.65 attendees per class — large enough to reverse the sign of the conclusion.
  • Review the delta at eight weeks and the absolute level again at sixteen. A positive change into a structurally dead slot still leaves you with a dead slot.
  • Report the sample size. An instructor with eight classes cannot support a conclusion in either direction.

What would falsify this report

  • Bottom-tier instructors improving without any intervention would mean the September effects were noise, not signal.
  • Client return rates converging across instructors once hosted classes are excluded would remove the retention-based recommendations.
  • The adjusted-effect measure failing to predict the next eight substitutions, having predicted the last 23 at r = 0.69, would undermine Report 01 Section B and Report 04 Section D together.
  • New-client conversion remaining at 9% after two full months of the second-visit prompt would point to the offer or the market rather than the process.

sections.title: Methodology, definitions and data limitations
sections.layout:
METHODOLOGY

Methodology, definitions and data limitations

Sources and reconciliation

  • Primary attendance source: the Checkins sheet of "Day End Report - Part 4" (member-level, 151,999 rows across all locations; 66,626 at Kwality House).
  • Secondary source: "Day End Report - Part 3 - Sessions" (session-level, 9,782 Kwality House rows, Jan 2024 – Oct 2026), used for capacity, bookings, late cancellations, revenue and format.
  • Reconciliation: September 2026 session-level check-ins (2,090) equal member-level check-in records (2,090) exactly. Bookings (2,325) equal check-ins plus late cancellations (234) in 327 of 328 classes.
  • Corroboration: "Day End Report - Part 1 - Payroll" teacher-month aggregates were used to cross-check class counts per instructor.

Definitions

  • Attendance / check-in: a member-level record with Checked In = TRUE. Bookings and reservations are never counted as attendance.
  • Utilisation: check-ins ÷ session capacity, summed at the level of aggregation. Capacity differs by format and by room (5–22), so utilisation and attendance answer different questions.
  • Late cancellation: Is Late Cancelled = TRUE. Net bookings = check-ins + late cancellations.
  • New client: Class No = 1, i.e. the member's first-ever recorded class.
  • Repeat client: a member with two or more check-ins with the same instructor in September.
  • Time bands: Early ≤07:45; Morning 08:00–09:45; Late morning 10:00–11:30; Midday 12:00–13:00; Afternoon 16:00–16:45; Evening 17:00–18:30; Late evening 18:45+.

Statistical approach

  • Fixed-effects model: OLS, 328 observations, instructor + day-of-week + time band + format + log(capacity) + ISO week. R² = 0.318. Instructor coefficients re-centred on the session-weighted roster average.
  • Why OLS and not a raw comparison: instructors are not randomly assigned to slots. Without controls, an instructor's average measures their timetable as much as their draw.
  • Head-to-head: restricted to recurring slots taught by ≥2 instructors with ≥2 classes each between March and September 2026, giving direct within-slot comparison with no modelling.
  • Affinity null model: 200 Monte Carlo reshuffles of instructor labels within each client's own visit history.

Limitations — read before acting

  • No-shows are not observable. The data records net bookings (check-ins plus late cancellations). Members who booked and simply did not arrive, and members who cancelled outside the late-cancellation window, do not appear. Late-cancellation rate is therefore a partial proxy for booking friction.
  • Waitlist and turned-away demand are not recorded. Where a class is full, we can see it is full but not how many members wanted a place. The Strength Lab opportunity in Report 02 is therefore a floor, not a ceiling.
  • Retention windows are truncated. Check-in data extends to 2026-10-21, so the post-September observation window is 24 days, not 30. All month-on-month retention comparisons in this report use a consistent 21-day window for this reason.
  • Small samples. Richard D'Costa (8 classes) and Anmol Sharma (14) cannot support strong conclusions; their confidence labels reflect this.
  • September contained an 11-day festival and a full closure day. See Report 02 for the decomposition. Instructor comparisons in this report control for week but not for festival phase; treat single-month instructor movements with appropriate caution.
  • Instructor effect is not the same as instructor quality in the presence of unobserved slot characteristics. Where a slot has been held by one instructor for a year, the model cannot fully separate the two.

subheadings: The finding that reframes the month
Year on year: where the growth went
Month on month: every format fell
The five findings that should change the schedule
sections.layout:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

September in context: a growth streak that stopped

Kwality House ran 328 classes across 29 operating days in September 2026 and recorded 2,090 check-ins at 45.4% capacity utilisation. Those are respectable numbers. They are also, on closer inspection, the moment a nine-month growth run came to a halt — and the cause is specific, measurable and fixable.

The finding that reframes the month

September 2026 produced 2,090 check-ins. September 2025 produced 2,110. After twelve months of growth the studio delivered one per cent less than the same month last year. August 2026, by contrast, was 46% ahead of August 2025 (2,593 vs 1,776). This is not a seasonal blip that averages out, and it is not explained by the Ganeshotsav festival alone — the decline began before the festival started. It is explained almost entirely by one format: powerCycle lost 148 check-ins year on year and 11.3 percentage points of utilisation, while Barre 57 gained 90 and Strength Lab gained 38. The studio did not have a bad September. It had a powerCycle September.

Year on year: where the growth went

Total check-ins by format, September 2025 versus September 2026. Barre and Strength Lab both grew; powerCycle fell by 26%.

Month on month: every format fell

Average attendance per class. Against the trailing three-month average, powerCycle fell 1.13 per class — more than twice the fall in Barre.

The five findings that should change the schedule

1 · powerCycle is in structural decline, not a September dip
Observation
powerCycle has fallen every month since mid-August and shows no sign of stabilising.
Evidence
Weekly average attendance per powerCycle class: 7.00 (week ending 16 Aug), 5.48, 5.19, 5.29, 4.76, 4.57, 4.72, 4.11 (week ending 4 Oct). Utilisation fell from 59.5% in June–August to 48.2% in September, and from 63.7% in September 2025. Three of the studio's four completely empty classes in September were powerCycle.
Interpretation
A decline that begins in mid-August, continues through a festival, and persists after it is not a calendar effect. Demand for this format is eroding.
Why it matters
powerCycle is still 26.5% of the schedule but only 20.0% of attendance. Eight of its twenty-one recurring slots average under 4.0 attendees.
Recommended action
Reduce powerCycle supply by roughly a third — cut the eight chronically sub-4.0 recurring slots first — and redeploy the floor time to Strength Lab and the high-yield Barre variants. Retain the five slots that work (Thursday 18:00, Tuesday 19:15, Wednesday 08:00, Wednesday 10:30, Saturday 10:00–11:30).
Expected outcome
Reallocating the 31 sub-4.0 powerCycle classes to formats at their own September averages is worth an estimated +128 to +151 check-ins per month on a like-for-like capacity basis.
Success metric
powerCycle utilisation back above 55% within two months on a reduced slot count; no recurring powerCycle slot below 4.0 average for six consecutive occurrences.
2 · Strength Lab is the studio’s only genuinely demand-constrained product — and it is capped at seven seats
Observation
Strength Lab runs at 82.4% utilisation with 40% of its classes completely full. The studio is turning people away and has no way to record it.
Evidence
57 classes, 338 check-ins, 410 places, 82.4% utilisation. 23 classes finished completely full and 41 reached 85% of capacity. In 18 of the 57 classes, net bookings exceeded room capacity. Utilisation has run at 82–83% for at least four consecutive months — this is a ceiling, not a peak.
Interpretation
At 82% utilisation with 40% of sessions sold out, marginal demand cannot be served. Every additional Strength Lab class at this fill rate adds roughly 5.8 check-ins that the studio currently cannot capture.
Why it matters
This is the only place in the schedule where adding supply demonstrably adds attendance rather than dividing it.
Recommended action
Add three Strength Lab classes per week in slots currently occupied by failing powerCycle classes: Monday 18:00, Thursday 10:30 and Wednesday 19:15. Install a waitlist so turned-away demand becomes measurable.
Expected outcome
Roughly +44 net check-ins per month after subtracting the attendance of the classes displaced, and a measurable waitlist within four weeks.
Success metric
Strength Lab utilisation sustained above 80% on the larger slot count, with waitlist volume recorded and reported weekly.
3 · The studio’s most-scheduled class is only its fourth best
Observation
Within the Barre family — 56% of the schedule — the allocation of class types does not match demonstrated demand.
Evidence
Studio Barre 57: 69 sessions at 6.43 average and 37.1% utilisation. Studio Mat 57: 22 sessions at 10.86 average and 54.3%. Studio FIT: 25 at 8.80 and 51.8%. Mat 57 draws 69% more people per class than Barre 57 from a third of the sessions.
Interpretation
Mat 57, FIT and Cardio Barre are under-scheduled relative to how clients actually vote. Barre 57 is the default filler.
Why it matters
Reallocating format within the same room, same instructor pool and same time slot is the cheapest change available — it requires no new capacity, no new hiring and no marketing.
Recommended action
Convert four weekly Studio Barre 57 classes in low-utilisation slots to Studio Mat 57 or Studio FIT, starting with Monday 07:15, Thursday 19:15, Tuesday 17:45 and Sunday 16:00.
Expected outcome
If conversion captures even 55% of the gap between Barre 57 and Mat 57 averages on four weekly classes, roughly +36 to +45 check-ins per month.
Success metric
Converted classes average ≥8.5 within six occurrences, and no neighbouring class in the same time slot falls by more than 1.5.
4 · Monday evening and Friday evening are structurally dead; Saturday late morning is structurally full
Observation
The weekly schedule is not aligned with where demand actually sits.
Evidence
Monday 17:00–18:30 averages 4.27 per class at 31.5% utilisation across 11 classes. Friday 18:45+ averages 3.17 at 27.5% utilisation across 6 classes — the worst cell in the studio, including one class with zero attendees. Saturday 10:00–11:30 averages 7.87 at 60.6% utilisation across 23 classes, the strongest window in the studio. Sunday runs only 8.0 classes per operating day against Monday’s 12.5.
Interpretation
Supply is concentrated on the days and hours with the weakest demand, and thin on the weekend late-morning window that demonstrably works.
Why it matters
Monday carries the highest daily class count (12.5) and the second-lowest average (5.80). That is 50 classes a month of below-average return.
Recommended action
Shift two to three classes per week out of Monday and Friday evenings into Saturday and Sunday late morning. Do not simply delete them — move them.
Expected outcome
Moved classes should deliver their new window’s average rather than their old one: a class worth 3.2 on Friday evening is worth roughly 7.9 on Saturday late morning.
Success metric
Saturday and Sunday late-morning utilisation sustained above 55% on the higher class count, and Monday evening utilisation above 40% on a reduced class count.
5 · Room capacity is mismatched to class demand on a third of the schedule
Observation
The same class type runs in rooms of 12, 20 and 22 seats depending on the slot, with no apparent relationship to how many people come.
Evidence
Studio Barre 57 ran at 12-seat capacity in six recurring slots and at 20–22 seats in six others. The 20–22 seat instances averaged 6.7; the 12-seat instances averaged 6.1 — essentially identical attendance in rooms of very different size, producing 31.9% versus 50.8% utilisation. Barre 57 as a whole fills 37.1% of the space it is given.
Interpretation
Attendance is set by demand for the slot, not by room size. Large rooms assigned to small classes create the appearance of terrible utilisation and consume space that high-demand formats could use.
Why it matters
Utilisation is the metric management is judged on, and a large share of the studio’s 54.6% unused capacity is a room-assignment artefact rather than a demand problem.
Recommended action
Establish a room-allocation rule: any recurring class averaging under 7 across four consecutive occurrences moves to the 12-seat room; the 20–22 seat rooms are reserved for Mat 57, FIT and Cardio Barre, which actually fill them.
Expected outcome
Reported utilisation rises without any change in attendance — this is a measurement correction — and the large rooms become available to formats that can use them.
Success metric
No recurring class in a 20+ seat room averaging below 7.0 for four consecutive occurrences; studio-reported utilisation recalculated on right-sized rooms.

Decomposing September: festival effect versus underlying softening

Ganeshotsav ran from 14 to 25 September 2026, and the studio was closed on the 25th. It would be easy to attribute the whole month to the festival. What the phases show

Average attendance fell from 7.46 in the 1–13 August baseline to 6.64 in the pre-festival 1–13 September window — a drop of 0.82 before the festival had begun. It then fell a further 0.69 during Ganeshotsav itself, to 5.95, and recovered to 6.67 in the five days after it. Two separate things happened: a pre-festival softening, and a festival effect that the studio then recovered from.

Cross-studio validation

Over the same three phases, Supreme HQ Bandra went 6.14 (Aug) → 5.98 (1–13 Sep) → 4.71 (14–25 Sep) → 5.59 (26–30 Sep) and Kenkere House went 5.36 → 4.79 → 4.06 → 4.69. All three studios dipped during the festival and all three recovered after it. But in the pre-festival window, Kwality fell 0.82 while Bandra fell only 0.16. The festival was city-wide; the early-September softening was largely Kwality’s own.

Bookings versus actual attendance

Conversion and cancellation

Of 2,325 net bookings, 2,090 converted to attendance (89.9%) and 234 were late cancellations (10.1%). The late-cancellation rate is the lowest recorded in twelve months (September 2025: 27.0%), which is not good news — it reflects thinner booking pipelines rather than better behaviour.

Critical caveat: the source data records net bookings after early cancellations. Members who booked and did not attend, and members who cancelled outside the late window, are not observable in either file. True no-show rate cannot be calculated.

Format diagnosis

Barre 57 — stable, dominant, and internally mis-allocated
Observation
Barre 57 is 56.1% of the schedule and 63.8% of attendance. Its aggregate performance barely moved: 7.46 average in June–August versus 7.24 in September, utilisation 42.2% versus 40.1%.
Evidence
But the aggregate hides real dispersion. Within the family, Mat 57 averages 10.86 and FIT 8.80, while Back Body Blaze averages 4.11, Cardio Barre Express 5.33, Mat 57 Express 5.43 and Recovery 3.00. The spread between the best and worst Barre variant is 3.6×.
Interpretation
Barre as a category is not the problem. The mix inside it is: the studio schedules its weakest-performing variants 27 times a month (Back Body Blaze, Express formats, Recovery, Cardio Barre Plus) and its strongest — Mat 57 — only 22 times.
Why it matters
These variants use the same rooms, the same instructors and the same client base. Changing the mix is close to free.
Recommended action
Protect and expand Mat 57 and FIT. Consolidate Back Body Blaze, Recovery and the Express variants into fewer slots, and move the surviving slots to the 12-seat room.
Expected outcome
A higher average per Barre class without any increase in class count.
Success metric
Barre family average above 7.8 and Barre utilisation above 45% within two months, on the same or fewer classes.
powerCycle — the studio’s central problem
Observation
powerCycle accounts for 26.5% of classes and 20.0% of attendance, and it is deteriorating on every measure.
Evidence
Average 4.816091954022989 versus 5.947761194029851 in June–August and 6.370786516853933 in September 2025. Utilisation 48.2% versus 59.5% and 63.7%. Three of the four empty classes. Highest late-cancellation rate at 13.6%. Eight of twenty-one recurring slots average under 4.0.
Interpretation
Two things are happening at once. First, the format as a whole has lost roughly a quarter of its year-ago demand. Second, the slots that remain are heavily concentrated on instructors with the weakest measured effects — Bret Saldanha (26 powerCycle classes at 3.77) and Raunak Khemuka (19 at 2.84) hold 45 of the 87 classes between them.
Why it matters
This single format explains the entire year-on-year stagnation of the studio. Fix nothing else and fix this.
Recommended action
Do not defend the current slot count. (1) Immediately withdraw the three structurally dead slots — Monday 18:00 (0.75 avg), Saturday 16:30 (2.00) and Friday 10:00 (2.00). (2) Convert Thursday 10:30 (2.50), Friday 08:30 (2.67) and Wednesday 19:15 (4.00) to Strength Lab. (3) Re-instructor Tuesday 07:30 (3.00) with Vivaran Dhasmana on a six-week test. (4) Retain and protect the five slots that work.
Expected outcome
Roughly 31 classes a month move from a 2.4 average to an expected 5.5–6.5, worth +95 to +125 check-ins per month net of displacement.
Success metric
powerCycle utilisation above 55% on the reduced slot count within two months; no recurring powerCycle slot below 4.0 for six consecutive occurrences.
Strength Lab — saturated, and the only place where more supply means more attendance
Observation
Strength Lab runs at 82.4% utilisation — nearly double Barre — with 40% of classes sold out.
Evidence
57 classes, 338 check-ins on 410 places. 23 classes full, 41 at 85%+. Standard deviation of attendance is just 1.19 — the most predictable product the studio has. Utilisation has held between 82% and 83% for four consecutive months, indicating a hard ceiling rather than a peak.
Interpretation
At this fill rate with a 7-seat room, marginal demand is being refused. The studio has no waitlist field in either data source, so the true size of the lost demand is unknown — which is itself a reporting gap worth closing.
Why it matters
Every other recommendation in this report involves moving demand around. This is the only one that grows it.
Recommended action
Add three Strength Lab classes per week, and install a waitlist so refused demand becomes visible. The 82% utilisation is achieved with almost no marketing and no promotional pricing.
Expected outcome
+44 net check-ins per month from the three added weekly classes, plus a measurable waitlist within four weeks.
Success metric
Strength Lab utilisation stays above 80% on the enlarged slot count; waitlist entries recorded weekly and reviewed monthly.

Do concurrent classes divide demand?

Of 269 distinct time slots in September, 213 ran a single class, 53 ran two and 3 ran three. Running two classes at once is associated with an average of 6.217 per class versus 6.441 for a single class — a dilution of 0.22 attendees per class, or about 3.5%. The dilution is real but small, and it is not a reason to avoid adding a class to a genuinely strong window. Where two concurrent classes both exceed 60% utilisation — Saturday 10:15, Tuesday 19:15 — the pair is capturing distinct demand, not splitting one pool.

Six inefficiencies the monthly report does not show

Weak formats are holding prime weekday-evening slots
Evidence
Monday 18:00 and 19:30 and Friday 19:00 and 19:15 are occupied by powerCycle and Cardio Barre Plus — four slots producing 4.75 attendees per class between them at 22% blended utilisation. Meanwhile Strength Lab, at 82% utilisation, has no Monday or Friday evening presence after 18:45.

Reallocate: one Monday evening and one Friday evening slot to Strength Lab.
The strongest Barre variants are confined to mornings and Saturdays
Evidence
Mat 57 runs at 10.86 average but appears only once after 17:00 in the entire month (Sunday 17:15, 9.25 average — which works). FIT appears after 17:00 only on Monday (8.25). The studio’s best Barre products are barely offered in the evening band.

Evidence
Sunday operates 8.0 classes per day against Monday's 12.5, yet Sunday's average attendance (6.84) beats Monday's (5.80) by 18%. Sunday late morning utilisation is 52.3% against Monday's 44.8%.
Action
Move two to three weekly classes from Monday to Sunday late morning.
Express and Recovery formats are consuming slots without earning them
Evidence
Cardio Barre Express (9 sessions, 5.33), Mat 57 Express (7, 5.43), Back Body Blaze Express (7, 6.71), PowerCycle Express (3, 4.67) and Recovery (4, 3.00) together account for 30 classes and 149 check-ins — 9.2% of the schedule for 7.1% of attendance, all at 15–47% utilisation.

Consolidate to no more than three Express slots per week, in the 12-seat room.
Room sizes are assigned without reference to demonstrated demand
Evidence
Studio Barre 57 runs in 12-seat rooms in six recurring slots (6.1 average, 51% utilisation) and in 20–22 seat rooms in six others (6.7 average, 32% utilisation). Same class, same demand, double the wasted space.

Adopt a right-sizing rule based on four-occurrence trailing averages.
Hosted corporate classes are inflating the headline
Evidence
Five hosted classes produced 60 check-ins (2.9% of the month) at zero recorded revenue and with a 21-day return rate far below the studio average. They are a marketing channel, not a retail product, and they distort every per-class metric they touch.

Report hosted classes as a separate line in the monthly pack.

sections.title: What the headline numbers are not telling us
sections.layout:
CRITICAL

What the headline numbers are not telling us

"2,090 check-ins" sounds like a normal month. It is a year of growth wiped out.
September 2025 produced 2,110 check-ins from 360 classes. September 2026 produced 2,090 from 328. Twelve months, 32 fewer classes, 20 fewer visits. August 2026 was 46% ahead of August 2025. The month-over-month slide from 2,593 to 2,090 is the story; the level is not.
"45.4% utilisation" is not 45.4% of anything meaningful.
Utilisation is computed on 4,606 places, but 410 of those places are in 7-seat Strength Lab rooms that run at 82% while 2,380 are in 18–20 seat Barre rooms that run at 37%. The blended figure describes the room mix, not the demand. 2,516 unused places is a headline; the actionable number is the 105 classes running below 35% utilisation.
"Barre is stable" is only true at the aggregate level.
Barre 57's average moved from 7.46 to 7.24 — but Mat 57 fell from 12.03 to 10.86, Thursday 19:15 Barre 57 fell from 10.92 to 5.75, and Tuesday 17:45 Barre 57 fell from 13.15 to 7.80. Two of the studio's historically strongest Barre classes lost roughly half their attendance. The stability is an average of gains and losses, not a steady state.
"powerCycle averages 4.82" hides that half of powerCycle works.
Thursday 18:00 powerCycle averages 8.75 at 88% utilisation; Wednesday 08:00 averages 7.60 at 76%; Tuesday 19:15 averages 7.60 at 76%. These are among the best classes in the studio. The format problem is concentrated in eight recurring slots — cutting powerCycle uniformly would destroy genuinely good classes.
"Only 4 empty classes" understates how close to empty many were.
4 classes had zero bookings, but 105 classes (32.0% of the schedule) ran below 35% utilisation and 23 ran at or below 20%. A 10-seat powerCycle with two people is commercially equivalent to empty but never appears in an empty-class count.
"Revenue per check-in of ₹910" is not evenly earned.
powerCycle generates ₹973 per check-in against Strength Lab’s ₹840 and Barre’s ₹908. powerCycle’s higher yield per head is real — which is exactly why cutting it must be selective, protecting the five productive slots and removing the eight dead ones.

How to read these four numbers

They are not additive. Opportunity 1 is a ceiling that overlaps heavily with 2 and 3. A realistic twelve-week target is the sum of opportunities 2, 3 and 4 at roughly 60% capture: about +165 to +175 check-ins per month, taking the studio from 2,090 to approximately 2,260. September 2026 was a festival-affected month, so the right comparison is not August’s 2,593 but August’s underlying run-rate: the 1–13 September pre-festival window ran at 6.64 per class, and 2,260 check-ins on a re-based schedule would represent roughly 7.2 per class — a genuine recovery above the pre-festival level. The highest-confidence component is opportunity 3, because it is the only one where the studio is presently refusing demand it can document.

sections.title: Methodology, definitions and data limitations
sections.layout:
METHODOLOGY

Methodology, definitions and data limitations

Sources and reconciliation

  • Checkins sheet ("Day End Report - Part 4", gid 0): 151,999 member-level booking records across all locations; 66,626 at Kwality House; 2,325 in September 2026.
  • Sessions extract ("Day End Report - Part 3 - Sessions"): 9,782 Kwality House session records, January 2024 to October 2026; 328 in September 2026.
  • Reconciliation: session-level check-ins (2,090) equal member-level records with Checked In = TRUE (2,090) exactly. Bookings (2,325) equal check-ins plus late cancellations (234) in 327 of 328 classes.
  • Four sessions had zero bookings and therefore no member-level records; they are retained in the session analysis as genuine empty classes, not treated as missing data.
  • Excluded: 33 placeholder records labelled "Unknown Class" (15 June – 13 August 2026, average attendance 0.1–0.4) that are system placeholders rather than real classes. None fall in September.

Definitions

  • Utilisation: check-ins ÷ the session’s own capacity, computed at the level of aggregation. Never a studio-wide capacity average.
  • Net bookings: check-ins + late cancellations, as recorded. Early cancellations are not present in either source.
  • Empty class: zero net bookings. Four in September.
  • Recurring slot: day + start time + format family. Strength Lab variants (Push, Pull, Full Body and the generic Strength Lab) are treated as one family because the studio consolidated them during August and September 2026 — see Report 04.
  • Time bands: Early ≤07:45; Morning 08:00–09:45; Late morning 10:00–11:30; Midday 12:00–13:00; Afternoon 16:00–16:45; Evening 17:00–18:30; Late evening 18:45+.
  • Operating day: a date on which at least one class ran. 29 in September; 25 September was a full closure.

Seasonal and calendar adjustments

  • Ganeshotsav ran 14–25 September 2026 (Ganesh Chaturthi 14 September; Anant Chaturdashi and visarjan 25 September). The studio recorded no sessions on 25 September.
  • September is therefore split into pre-festival (1–13), festival (14–25) and post-festival (26–30) phases throughout this report, with an August baseline for comparison.
  • Cross-studio comparison against Supreme HQ Bandra and Kenkere House is used to separate city-wide calendar effects from studio-specific ones.
  • September 2025 and September 2024 are used as seasonal comparators where the month-on-month comparison could be confounded by the festival.

Limitations — read before acting

  • No-shows are not observable. Neither source records members who booked and did not attend, or who cancelled outside the late-cancellation window. Late-cancellation rate is a partial proxy only.
  • Waitlist and refused demand are not recorded. Where a class is full we can see it is full but not how many were turned away. The Strength Lab opportunity is therefore a documented floor, not a ceiling.
  • Room identity is not available, only capacity. Room-allocation recommendations are inferred from capacity patterns; confirm against the actual room schedule before implementing.
  • October 2026 is incomplete in the source data and is used only for retention windows, never as a benchmark month.
  • Opportunity 1 (+385) is a statistical ceiling, not a forecast. It assumes demand materialises in classes that have been weak for months. It is included to size the prize, not to set a target.
  • Revenue figures come from the session extract; hosted classes show zero revenue and should not be read as generating none.

Observation
Cash collected reached ₹3,206,431 — the second-highest month in thirteen, and 27.4% above September 2025. Transactions fell to 272, the lowest count in the series.
Evidence
A single transaction (Sale ID 325708785, 14 Sep, 10 × Studio Private Class X 10 at ₹42,000) contributed ₹420,000 — 13.1% of the month. Remove it and September is ₹2,786,431: −7.0% against August and +10.7% against September 2025. Meanwhile attendance fell from 2,593 to 2,090 (−19.4%) and the renewal rate fell to 59.8%, its worst in twelve months.
Interpretation
The headline is a composition effect, not growth. Fewer people bought more expensive things. Average value per sale rose 50.2% MoM (₹7,846 → ₹11,788) purely because the mix shifted from ₹1,942 drop-ins toward annual memberships and private packages.
Why it matters
If September is reported as a record month, October will be planned against a base that includes a one-off ₹420,000 private sale that has not recurred in the prior twelve months. The plan would be built on ₹420,000 of revenue that does not exist.
Action
Report September two ways, every month. Publish "Total collected" and "Collected excluding single sales above ₹200,000" side by side. Set the October plan off the adjusted figure (₹2.79m), not the headline (₹3.21m).
Expected outcome
October planned against a realistic base; no false shortfall created by an artefact.
Success metric
Adjusted monthly revenue tracked as the primary series; variance to plan ≤ 5% in Q4.

The five numbers that should drive October

  • ₹2,786,431 — September revenue excluding the one-off private sale. This is the run-rate, not ₹3.21m.
  • 272 transactions — the lowest in thirteen months, down 22.3% year on year. Fewer people are buying.
  • 59.8% — the September paid-membership renewal rate, down from 75.7% in October 2025. The base is eroding while ticket size grows.
  • ₹1,534 — revenue per check-in, up 32.7% MoM. The studio is earning more from each visit and seeing fewer visits.
  • ₹1,304,458 — cash collected above revenue recognised (₹3.21m vs ₹1.90m). Deferred revenue is building; that liability is future attendance that has already been paid for.

Revenue is now decoupled from attendance — and that is a warning, not a win
Observation
Over the last eight months cash collected per check-in has risen from ₹1,001 (Feb 2026) to ₹1,534 (Sep 2026), a 53% increase, while monthly check-ins fell from 2,593 to 2,090.
Evidence
Cash per check-in by month: Feb ₹1,001 · Mar ₹884 · Apr ₹2,310 · May ₹1,053 · Jun ₹956 · Jul ₹1,061 · Aug ₹1,156 · Sep ₹1,534. Recognised revenue per check-in moved far less, from ₹744 (Feb) to ₹910 (Sep), +22%.
Interpretation
Two separate things are happening. First, price realisation genuinely improved — members are paying more per visit than they did in February. Second, and more concerning, cash is arriving for visits that have not happened yet. The gap between cash and recognised revenue widened to ₹1,304,458 in September, the largest in the series.
Why it matters
Rising cash per check-in looks like pricing power. Much of it is deferred revenue — money banked against future attendance. If that attendance never materialises, the studio has sold capacity it must now deliver, into a schedule that is already running at 45.4% utilisation with falling footfall.
Action
Institute a monthly deferred-revenue roll-forward. Track opening balance, new sales, recognised consumption, and closing balance by product line. Report consumption rate (sessions used ÷ sessions sold in the trailing 90 days) alongside revenue.

Visibility on whether September sales convert into October–December attendance or expire unused.
Success metric
Deferred revenue balance and its 90-day consumption rate reported monthly; consumption rate ≥ 70%.

Unlimited members are paying for three visits a week and using one. The churn analysis in Report 07 shows members completing 11 or more sessions renew at 87.0% against 50.9% for those completing one to four.

Every rupee of the September margin improvement comes from members not using what they bought. That is not a durable revenue model; it converts into lapsed renewals one to three months later.

Target consumption, not sales. Set a 30-day activation target of 6 visits for every new unlimited member and 3 for package holders. Assign the 63 active memberships expiring within 14 days to a named associate with a usage review before the renewal conversation.

Retail items are bars, drinks and small-format nutrition (SQ Raw Granola Bar, Cacao & Maca Ball, Impact Water 350ML). Vahishta: 63 items, ₹924,177, ₹14,669 avg. Akshay: 61 items, ₹870,953, ₹14,278 avg. Tahira: 66 items, ₹527,857, ₹7,998 avg. Sheetal: 38 items, ₹527,620, ₹13,885 avg. Tahira sells 45% more transactions than Sheetal for the same revenue.
Interpretation
This is an assignment pattern, not a capability gap. The high-ticket products — annual memberships, private packages, multi-month commitments — are concentrated in two sellers. A seller handling drop-ins, retail and single sessions cannot reach a ₹14,000 average ticket no matter how well they sell; ₹1,942 is the price of the product.
Why it matters
If the studio ranks sellers on revenue, it will conclude Tahira is underperforming by 43% when she is in fact handling nearly half the transaction volume. Ranking on revenue alone will push the team away from the small transactions that keep frequency high.
Action
Report sellers on revenue and on transactions side by side, and equalise access to high-ticket leads. Route every enquiry that mentions annual, private or multi-month to a rotating queue rather than to a named individual. Give each seller a monthly high-ticket target (≥ ₹50,000 items) alongside their volume target.
Expected outcome
More even distribution of high-value selling opportunities; a fairer and more diagnostic scorecard.
Success metric
Spread between highest and lowest average ticket narrowing from 1.83× to below 1.4× within two quarters, without any seller losing total revenue.

09

Cash Collected vs Revenue Earned

The studio collected ₹3.21m in September and delivered ₹1.90m of sessions. The ₹1.30m difference is a promise the schedule has to keep.

What the two numbers mean

  • ₹3,206,431 — cash invoiced in September (Sales file). This is money in the door.
  • ₹1,901,973 — value of sessions actually attended in September (session ledger). This is revenue earned.
  • ₹1,304,458 — the net increase in deferred revenue. Members bought entitlements they have not yet used.
  • 2,090 check-ins were delivered against 4,606 seats scheduled. There is 2,516 seats of unused capacity in the month to absorb future consumption.

Utilisation headroom

45.4% utilisation. Even if every entitlement sold in September were redeemed within 30 days, the September schedule could absorb it. The constraint on converting deferred revenue into earned revenue is not capacity — it is member behaviour.

Deferred revenue is rising faster than the studio can see
Observation
The gap between cash collected and revenue recognised has widened in six of the last twelve months and reached ₹1,304,458 in September, the largest in the series.
Evidence
Monthly gap (cash − recognised): Oct-25 ₹1,356,065 · Nov-25 ₹292,233 · Dec-25 ₹1,100,698 · Jan-26 ₹1,211,292 · Feb-26 ₹492,956 · Mar-26 ₹333,726 · Apr-26 ₹3,373,001 · May-26 ₹642,958 · Jun-26 ₹469,589 · Jul-26 ₹643,937 · Aug-26 ₹731,260 · Sep-26 ₹1,304,458.
Interpretation
Cumulatively the studio has banked substantially more entitlement than members are consuming. April 2026 alone added ₹3.37m of deferred revenue. Consumption is running at roughly 60% of sales value per month.
Why it matters
Deferred revenue is not profit. It is an obligation to deliver a service. If members lapse before consuming — and the September renewal rate of 59.8% says 40% of them do — the studio keeps the cash but loses the relationship and the future. Conversely, if consumption accelerates, the 45.4% utilisation schedule must absorb it.
Action
Build a monthly deferred-revenue schedule by product line with an expiry profile. Flag entitlements expiring within 30 days and contact those members with a use-it-or-renew prompt. Report the balance to the owner monthly.
Expected outcome
Deliberate management of the largest untracked liability in the business.
Success metric
Deferred-revenue balance tracked monthly with a 30-day expiry report; consumption rate (trailing-90-day sessions used ÷ sessions sold) reported and held above 70%.

10

Hidden Patterns

Six things the monthly total does not show.

1. The median transaction is ₹1,942, the mean is ₹11,788 — a 6.1× gap

114 of 272 line items (41.9%) were single sessions or format drop-ins priced at ₹1,942.50. They produced ₹225,880 — 7.0% of revenue. The mean is pulled up by 4 annuals, 11 private packages and 41 class packages. Any target expressed as "average transaction value" will be dominated by the four or five largest sales of the month and will move for reasons that have nothing to do with front-desk performance. Track the median and the count of items above ₹50,000 instead.

2. Money credits are being loaded, not spent — ₹6,226 across 21 transactions

21 line items loaded money credits at an average of ₹296. Money credits are stored value: they are a liability, not revenue, until redeemed. The loaded amount is trivial in September, but the mechanism matters because it is the only prepayment product in the file that does not expire with a membership. Money-credit balances are not tracked in any source provided and should be reported separately from revenue.

3. Point of sale takes 93.9% of revenue but the digital channels have a 2.1× lower ticket

POS: 239 items, ₹3,010,553, ₹12,575 avg. Checkout pages: 18 items, ₹126,814, ₹7,045 avg. Mobile app: 15 items, ₹69,064, ₹4,604 avg. Self-serve buyers buy drop-ins; the desk sells commitments. The digital channel is not a lower-cost substitute for the desk — it is a different, smaller-ticket product mix. Any plan to shift sales online without changing what is offered there will reduce revenue per transaction.

4. September has two clear campaign spikes and 27 quiet days

Day 1 (₹783,766, 24.4%) and day 14 (₹515,366, 16.1%) together are 40.5% of the month. The remaining 27 days averaged ₹70,700 each. September was two campaigns and a base business of roughly ₹1.9m. The base business, not the ₹3.21m, is what October inherits.

5. Discounting is concentrated: two codes are 78.6% of all discount given

OTTWENTEE (₹167,200) and PR1V@TE20 (₹100,000) account for ₹267,200 of ₹340,365 total. The other seven codes cost ₹73,165 across 34 line items. Discount governance is a two-code problem. Approving those two codes deliberately would control four-fifths of total discount spend.

6. Cash is 31.6% of collections — ₹1,013,197 across 68 line items

This is a material cash-handling exposure and a reconciliation burden. It also matters for autorenew: the churn analysis in Report 07 finds only 30 of 208 active memberships have a card on file. A business taking a third of its money in cash cannot switch on recurring billing without first running a card-capture programme.

Recommendations

Six actions, sequenced. Each states the arithmetic behind it and the measure that will tell you it worked.

A1. Report revenue two ways: headline and adjusted

P1 · This week · Owner: Studio manager

Publish monthly collections alongside collections excluding any single sale above ₹200,000. September: ₹3,206,431 headline, ₹2,786,431 adjusted, a 13.1% difference from one transaction. Plan October against ₹2.79m.

Execution: Monthly revenue report carries both figures; October plan built on the adjusted series.

Success metric: Variance between actual and planned revenue ≤ 5% for three consecutive months.

A2. Build a deferred-revenue roll-forward with an expiry profile

P1 · Two weeks · Owner: Studio manager + finance

September added ₹1,304,458 of deferred revenue. Open a simple schedule: opening balance, new sales, consumption, expiries, closing balance, by product line. Report entitlements expiring in 30 days and contact those members.

Execution: Monthly deferred-revenue statement; 30-day expiry contact list actioned.

Success metric: Trailing-90-day consumption rate (sessions used ÷ sessions sold) reported and ≥ 70%.

A3. Attack consumption, not sales volume

P1 · Two weeks · Owner: Front-desk leads

474 clients averaged 4.41 visits. Members completing 11+ sessions renew at 87.0% versus 50.9% for 1–4 sessions (Report 07, n=2,087). Set a 6-visit first-30-day target for new unlimited members and 3 for package holders; review at day 21.

Execution: Per-member consumption dashboard; named associate owns each new member's first 30 days.

Success metric: Median monthly visits per active member from 4.41 to 5.2; renewal rate from 59.8% to 68%.

A4. Schedule the annual-membership offer twice a year

P2 · Six weeks · Owner: Owner + marketing

Four annuals sold in six hours on 1 September at 20% off produced ₹702,240 for a discount cost of ₹175,600 — a 4:1 return. Repeat deliberately; test 15% before assuming 20% is required.

Execution: Two defined annual-offer windows per year with a code, a date and a target.

Success metric: Annual memberships sold per window ≥ 4; annual line at a stable 12–15% of monthly revenue.

A5. Fix the seller scorecard and equalise high-ticket lead routing

P2 · Four weeks · Owner: Sales lead

Top seller ₹14,669 average ticket, bottom ₹7,998 — a gap driven by product assignment, not skill. Report revenue and transaction count together. Route annual, private and multi-month enquiries through a rotating queue.

Execution: Dual-metric scorecard live; rotating queue for enquiries above ₹50,000.

Success metric: Average-ticket spread between sellers from 1.83× to below 1.4× with no loss of total revenue.

A6. Govern the two discount codes that are 79% of discount spend

P2 · Four weeks · Owner: Owner

OTTWENTEE (₹167,200) and PR1V@TE20 (₹100,000) are 78.6% of ₹340,365 total discount. Require named approval for any code above ₹50,000 of monthly spend. Correct any dashboard that sums the sale-level discount column — it overstates September discounting 3.7×.

Execution: Approval threshold in place; discount reporting reconciled to the per-line column.

Success metric: Effective discount rate held at or below 7% of list value excluding scheduled campaigns.

What these six add up to

  • Protects the plan from a ₹420,000 phantom (A1) — a planning correction, not new revenue.
  • Recovers renewal rate from 59.8% toward 68% (A3). At 174 resolved expiries a month and an average lapsed value of ₹11,738, an 8.2pp recovery retains roughly 14 memberships a month — about ₹168,000 of membership value, plus their ongoing consumption.
  • Adds roughly ₹48,500 a month from retail attach at 30% (Report 06 §6) and an estimated ₹40,000–₹60,000 a month from a repeatable annual offer (A4).
  • Controls ₹267,200 of annualised discount spend through two approval decisions (A6).
  • Prevents the largest reporting error available in the current data: a 3.7× overstatement of discounting (A6).

Confidence: A1, A5 and A6 are High — directly measurable in reconciled data. A2 is High for the measurement and Moderate for the response. A3 is Moderate — the consumption–renewal relationship is strong (n=2,087) but causal. A4 is Moderate — one observed campaign, one month, no control. Detailed sensitivity is in Report 07 §11 and Report 09 §9.

sections.title: Methodology, Reconciliation & Limitations
subheadings: Limitations — the five that matter most
sections.layout:
12

Methodology, Reconciliation & Limitations

Every figure above, traceable to source.

Sources and scope

  • Primary: Sales – Raw – Sales (23).csv — 25,044 rows, 49 columns, payments at line-item grain, 4 Jul 2023 to 10 Oct 2026. 10,330 rows for Kwality House, Kemps Corner.
  • Supporting: Day End Report session ledger (328 September sessions) for attendance, capacity and recognised revenue; Bookings sheet (2,549 de-duplicated September bookings) for attendance mix.
  • Period: 1–30 September 2026. Twelve-month context uses October 2025 to September 2026; thirteen-month charts add September 2025 for year-on-year.
  • Studio: Kwality House, Kemps Corner only. Filtered on Calculated Location, never on a name pattern.

Reconciliation

  • 3 rows removed from 10,330: 2 with payment status other than succeeded and 1 voided. 10,327 rows retained.
  • Discounting is measured on "Sale Item Unit Discount Value", not "Discount Value In Currency". The latter repeats the sale-level total on each line of a multi-line sale; summing it yields ₹1,265,715 for September against a true ₹340,365. The per-line column reconciles exactly to the sale-level total on every single-line sale and to the sale total when summed across the 10 lines of the one large private sale.
  • Nine category totals sum to ₹3,206,431, matching the file total exactly.
  • Attributed seller revenue (₹2,991,129) plus unattributed (₹215,302) equals the month total. 35 line items carry no seller.
  • Attendance: session ledger 2,090 check-ins; checkins file 2,090 with Checked In = TRUE; Bookings sheet 1,941 after de-duplication. The 149 gap is documented in Report 08 §3.

Definitions

  • Cash collected — sum of Payment Value, which is the net amount paid after discount. Verified: on every discounted line, Payment Value equals unit price minus unit discount.
  • List value — cash collected plus discount. Discount rate — discount ÷ list value.
  • Average value per sale — revenue ÷ distinct Sale ID (₹13,762). Per line item — revenue ÷ rows (₹11,788). Both are reported because the source is at line-item grain and a single sale may carry 10 rows.
  • Recognised revenue — Revenue on the session ledger, being the value of sessions consumed. A different measure from cash; the difference is deferred revenue.
  • Renewal rate — renewals ÷ (renewals + lapses) for paid memberships expiring in the month, excluding frozen. Source and full method in Report 07.

Limitations — the five that matter most

  • No cost data exists in any source. No instructor rates, rent, or product cost. Every margin statement in this report is inference from price and mix, not measured profitability. This is the largest gap.
  • Recognised revenue is supplied, not derived. The session ledger provides a Revenue figure per class with no stated allocation method. The deferred-revenue gap is therefore as reliable as that field, and should be confirmed against the studio's own accounting.
  • Discount attribution is imperfect. 35 line items carry no seller and 1 line item carries no discount code. Discount by seller cannot be computed reliably and is not reported.
  • October 2026 is partial (1–10 October only). It is used for the win-back window in Report 07 and nowhere as a benchmark.
  • Refunds are not netted. The file carries a refund flag but no refund amounts against September Kwality House line items; revenue here is gross of any subsequent refund.

A note on confidence labels

High confidence means the finding is directly measurable in the reconciled data with a stable sample. Moderate means the direction is well supported but the magnitude rests on an assumption stated in the text. Low means the finding depends on behaviour the data cannot observe; no such item is presented as fact anywhere in this report.
